title: Kittl Alternatives Worth Switching To
summary: Kittl alternatives compared on which plan exports SVG and PDF and what each license lets you sell, from free Affinity and Inkscape to Illustrator.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Kittl's Free plan exports PNG and JPG at up to 800px and 72dpi, and SVG and PDF start on Pro, at $14 a month billed annually or $19 monthly.
- Six of the nine Kittl alternatives after ours confirm SVG export in their docs, and three of them export SVG on a $0 plan: Affinity, Inkscape, and Recraft, whose Free images are public and can't be sold.
- Five of those six get you an SVG for less than Kittl Pro on either billing basis; only Illustrator, at $22.99 a month, costs more.
- Kittl's Pro and Expert licenses cap commercial use at 500,000 printed copies or expected viewers per design, and Free designs can't be sold at all.


The best Kittl alternatives for merch, print and social work come down to two questions: which plan hands you a print-ready vector file, and what the license lets you sell. Kittl puts both answers behind a paid plan.


Prices are US prices as of November 13, 2026; several vendors, Kittl included, charge differently elsewhere.


[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) comes first because it's our product. Behind it come the tools whose own docs confirm SVG export, ordered by the cheapest US plan that exports SVG and lets you sell the result, free first. Tools that don't itemize SVG export by plan, then those without it, come last, each by price.


## Why Kittl users go looking elsewhere


Export is the first wall. On Free, Kittl exports PNG and JPG "up to 800px and 72dpi", and its help center says "Vector and high-res exports require a paid plan". Pro, Expert and Max add PNG and JPG up to 10,800px at 300dpi plus SVG and PDF with transparent backgrounds, though CMYK comes "only ... for PDF and JPEG", and SVG always exports in RGB.


Kittl prices each paid plan per editor: Pro is $14 a month billed annually, or $19 monthly, and Expert is $39 or $49, and Max $65 or $85, on the same terms. Its cancellation page adds that "Refunds are generally not provided", so an annual plan is a year-long bet.


AI tokens are the second complaint. Kittl moved from credits to tokens in 2025: Pro gets 2,000 a month, Expert 12,000 (6,000 monthly plus 200 a day) and Max 30,000 (12,000 plus 600 a day). The pricing page calls daily credits "promotional and available for a limited time", so by our reading half of Expert's tokens and 18,000 of Max's are promotional, and included tokens don't roll over.


The allowance has moved before. In an[October 2024 r/KittlDesign thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/KittlDesign/comments/1g8bwwb/upcoming_credit_reduction_discussion/) , a user reported Expert's monthly credits dropping from 2,400 to 600 on December 1, 2024, at the same price, and replies asked about alternatives. It's one anecdotal Reddit report. Tokens only pay off on the design jobs AI handles well, the split we cover in[using AI for graphic design](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/using-ai-for-graphic-design) .


Performance on big files is the third reason. A print-on-demand designer wrote in a[December 2024 r/canva thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/canva/comments/1hjy1ei/canva_performance_question_tired_of_kittl/) that 20 or more artboards made Kittl lag 5 seconds or longer, and that an annual plan brought no refund. Anecdotal again, but Kittl's own page confirms the refund part.


Kittl keeps shipping, though. On July 2, 2026, its Apps panel added a Printful app that sends a design to Printful as a print file, and on September 17 Kittl connected to ChatGPT, Claude and Cursor. If Printful prints your products, that app is a fair reason to stay.


## Kittl alternatives compared on vector export


The last column, which plan gets you an SVG or a PDF, is what this list is ranked on.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Read the license notes in each entry as well, since an SVG you're not allowed to sell won't help a merch shop.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** Assets you'd rather not make


**Overview:** Awesomic has no vector editor, and our pages don't describe SVG, PDF or CMYK export. We're for the Kittl user who wants the assets made, not another canvas.


You describe the job in a chat, and our agents generate the artwork with image models. For print, the separate Graphic Pack puts a part-time designer, drawn from 200+ vetted experts across 30+ skill sets, on packaging, print, ads, emails and everyday graphics.


Either way, under our Subscription Terms we assign you our rights in AI Output once that billing cycle's fees are paid, and you can download your files for 30 days after canceling.


**Key features:**


- Nano Banana, GPT Image and FLUX on one bill.
- Brand memory of the files and decisions you've approved.
- 200+ templates to start a set from.
- Parallel agents on shared project files.


**Pricing:** Light costs $19 a month for each person and sets their monthly AI budget at the same $19; Basic, Pro and Studio are $99, $199 and $499. Agentic plans bill monthly and aren't refundable.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


By our math, one person on Light pays $219 a month before seat fees. The Graphic Pack is a separate $1,799 plan with its own Light subscription, $1,999 with the fee; whether that Light draws a second fee isn't stated, so read the checkout total.


**Pros:** Image models and templates in one place, one brand memory, a part-time print designer on the separate Graphic Pack


**Cons:** AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**How to start using it:**


1. Pick Light for agent-made assets, or the Graphic Pack if you need a print designer.
2. Name a project after the drop and add your logo and past designs.
3. Describe each product, from the shirt graphic to the launch posts.
4. Review drafts and share the project link for sign-off.
5. On the Graphic Pack, hand print tasks to your designer in the same chat.


**What you hand off instead:** The making itself, from first draft to print work.


**Final verdict:** Pick Awesomic to have social and merch assets made for you, moving to the separate $1,799 Graphic Pack when print needs a designer. To draw and export vectors yourself, Affinity or Inkscape gives you SVG and PDF free.


[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) on Light, or the Graphic Pack if print comes first.


### 2. Affinity


**Overview:** Affinity belongs to Canva now, and Canva calls it "free for individuals" on Mac, Windows and iPad. You sign in with a free Canva account.


For print, the free app exports SVG and PDF, including PDF/X-1a, X-3 and X-4, with CMYK, spot colors, preflight and bleed. It also imports PSD, AI, PDF, SVG and IDML files, which helps when a printer sends you something to fix.


**Key features:**


- PDF/X export with bleed, the file standard print shops ask for.
- Preflight checks before a run, plus spot colors for exact brand inks.
- PSD, AI and IDML import for files that started in other tools.


**Pricing:** Affinity is $0 with no paid tier. You'd pay for a Canva plan only to use Canva AI inside it.


**Pros:** SVG and PDF free, CMYK and spot colors, opens AI and IDML files


**Cons:** Not a browser app, its terms license the software to "a private individual" and point organizations to Canva Enterprise or Education, no Kittl-style template library that we found


**Why it's a good Kittl alternative:** It gives you, at no cost, the vector and CMYK print export Kittl keeps behind Pro, and the terms don't restrict your own output.


**Final verdict:** Choose Affinity if you draw your own designs and want press-ready PDFs without a subscription, and check the terms first if you're buying for a company.


### 3. Inkscape


**Overview:** Inkscape is open source under the GPL, and version 1.4.4 shipped in May 2026 for Windows, Mac and Linux. SVG is its native format, so every file you save is already a vector, and it also saves PDF, EPS and more.


Its ownership answer is the simplest here: files you make are "owned by the creators of the work", with no plan or print cap involved. The catch is color: its FAQ says it "currently does not support color management for file export".


**Key features:**


- Native SVG, so nothing gets converted on the way out.
- PDF and EPS saves for printers that want them.
- Free desktop builds for Windows, Mac and Linux.


**Pricing:** Inkscape is free, with no paid plan. That puts SVG and PDF at $0, against $14 a month billed annually for Kittl Pro.


**Pros:** SVG native, PDF free, files that belong to you with no copy cap


**Cons:** No color-managed CMYK export, desktop only, a steeper learning curve than Kittl's templates in our judgment


**The license advantage:** Your right to the file never depends on a subscription or an open account, unlike Kittl's rule for designs after a Pro or Expert plan ends.


**Final verdict:** Pick Inkscape for logos and merch art you want to own outright, and hand the CMYK step to another tool or your printer when a job needs it.


### 4. CorelDRAW Go


**Overview:** CorelDRAW Go took over from Corel Vector, which shut down, and it runs in the browser on a single plan. That plan exports JPG, PNG, WEBP, PDF or SVG, so vector output isn't a higher tier. Its templates run from logos and business cards to coffee mugs, and Corel lists merchandise, stickers and clothing among what you can make.


That makes it the closest drawing tool here to Kittl's merch focus. The hardware rules are strict, though: you need Chrome or Edge 142 or later (Firefox 146 has limited support) and 8 GB of RAM, and "touch screens and stylus are not supported", so tablet sketching is out.


**Key features:**


- Templates from logos and business cards to mugs and social posts.
- SVG and PDF export on the one plan.
- 1,000 AI credits a month.


**Pricing:** Monthly billing is $9.99 per 30 days, and the annual plan is $99.99 a year, with a Black Friday discount on the first period as of November 13, 2026. There's no free plan, but the 15-day free trial asks for no card.


**Pros:** SVG and PDF on its one plan, templates from logos to mugs, a trial without a card


**Cons:** No free plan, needs Chrome or Edge 142+ and 8 GB of RAM, no touch or stylus support


**The template case:** You keep template-led work, mugs included, and pay $9.99 per 30 days for SVG, against Kittl Pro's $19 monthly.


**Final verdict:** Choose CorelDRAW Go if you liked starting from Kittl's templates and want cheaper vector export, and check Corel's terms before a template design goes on a shirt as-is.


### 5. Recraft


**Overview:** Recraft generates vectors from text prompts, which suits the Kittl user who mostly prompts rather than draws. It exports PNG, JPG, TIFF, PDF, SVG and Lottie, and its docs say "Vector images can be exported as SVG and PDF".


Your plan decides what you can do with the result. Free still exports SVG, but its images are public, owned by Recraft and marked "No commercial use", so none of them can go on a product you sell. Paid plans give "full ownership and commercial rights" plus private generation, and that's why we place Recraft at its Basic price rather than at $0.


**Key features:**


- Text-to-vector generation.
- SVG, PDF and Lottie export for print and motion.
- Private generation on paid plans, so nobody sees a design before you launch it.


**Pricing:** Basic is $10 a month billed annually, or $12 monthly, for 1,000 credits, and Pro is $16 billed annually, or $20 monthly, for 2,000. Monthly credits don't roll over.


**Pros:** Vector generation from text, SVG and PDF export, commercial rights from Basic


**Cons:** Free images are public and owned by Recraft, credits don't roll over, a generator rather than a template or merch layout tool


**For prompt-first designers:** It replaces Kittl's AI tokens with output you can open as a vector and sell from $12 a month.


**Final verdict:** Pick Recraft if you generate most of your art, and lay it out on products in another tool.


### 6. Canva


**Overview:** Canva, which also owns Affinity, works the way Kittl does: open a template, swap the copy, export. For print, Canva says "CMYK color profile options, and transparent PNG/SVG are available to Canva Pro" and to its team, education and nonprofit plans, and its PDF Print option adds bleed and crop marks.


Two limits matter for merch. Canva gives you freehand and shape tools rather than a pen-and-node vector editor, and its license is direct about library elements: "You can't take an element from the Canva library... put it on a t-shirt, and sell it".


**Key features:**


- A large template library for social posts and print pieces.
- PDF Print with bleed and crop marks for printers.
- CMYK and transparent PNG on Pro.


**Pricing:** Pro is $144 a year for one person by default, or $18 a month billed monthly. Business is $250 a year per person.


**Pros:** Template-first like Kittl, SVG and CMYK on Pro, print PDFs with bleed


**Cons:** SVG, transparent PNG and CMYK all need Pro, no pen-and-node editing, library elements can't be sold as-is on merch


**Why it's a good Kittl alternative:** You keep the template-first habit, and Pro's $144 a year comes to $12 a month, under Kittl Pro's $14 billed annually.


**Final verdict:** Choose Canva for social graphics and print pieces built from templates, with your own art on anything you sell.


### 7. Adobe Illustrator


**Overview:** Illustrator is a full vector editor that exports SVG, PDF and its own AI format, which Affinity can open. It's built for drawing paths by hand, so expect to start most designs from a blank artboard.


Its type license is the strongest merch argument it has. Adobe says Adobe Fonts can be used on merchandise for commercial sale with "no restrictions on the number of impressions or items", so the fonts never become the limit on a print run.


**Key features:**


- SVG, PDF and AI export on its one plan.
- Adobe Fonts cleared for merch you sell, with no item limit.
- Adobe Express Premium included with the subscription.


**Pricing:** Illustrator is $22.99 a month on the annual plan, billed monthly, and that includes Adobe Express Premium. You get a 7-day trial and no free plan, so run a full print job through it inside that week.


**Pros:** Full vector drawing, SVG, PDF and AI export, Adobe Fonts with no merch item limit


**Cons:** No free plan, the $22.99 price needs an annual commitment, no template-first workflow


**What the higher price buys:** Unlimited merch use of Adobe Fonts and a real drawing tool, with Express Premium on the side for quick social work.


**Final verdict:** Pick Illustrator if you draw for a living and want Adobe Fonts cleared for merch, and accept the year-long commitment.


### 8. Linearity


**Overview:** Linearity Curve, formerly Vectornator, is still sold, and it's a vector editor with a free plan. Curve lists PDF, SVG and AI among its vector formats.


What we can't confirm is which plan exports them. The pricing page says only that Free has "Basic export options" and Pro has "Advanced export options". A Linearity blog post files SVG and PDF under "Advanced Export Options", which suggests a paid plan, so Linearity sits after the tools that itemize them.


Licensing is clearer. Linearity's FAQ says its free plan is "intended for hobbyists" and that a commercial license comes with paid plans, though the pricing page doesn't say which plan covers merch.


**Key features:**


- A vector editor in Curve, with PDF, SVG and AI listed as formats.
- 600 credits on Pro, with free welcome credits to try first.
- Curve apps for Mac, iPad and iPhone.


**Pricing:** Linearity's Pro runs $10 on monthly billing, or $8 a month paid yearly, while Studio starts at $30 monthly, or $25 a month paid yearly. The free welcome credits expire after 7 days.


**Pros:** A free plan to learn on, low Pro pricing, real vector editing


**Cons:** The export gate isn't documented by plan, free welcome credits expire in 7 days, several features are marked "Coming soon"


**Test it if:** You want a cheap vector editor and can check SVG export on Free in your first session.


**Final verdict:** Try Linearity free and export a test SVG before you pay, since its own pricing page won't tell you.


### 9. Adobe Express


**Overview:** Adobe Express is Adobe's template app for quick social graphics, and its Free plan exports JPEG, PNG, PDF, GIF, PPT and transparent PNG. Every plan gets Firefly AI that Adobe calls "designed to be commercially safe", which covers generated content rather than templates, so read Adobe's license before a template design goes on merch you sell.


What Express lacks is native SVG export of a design. Its Convert to SVG action only converts a JPG or PNG you upload, which isn't the same as exporting your layout as a vector, so a merch file that has to scale needs another tool.


**Key features:**


- PDF and transparent PNG on Free.
- Firefly generative AI on every plan, Free included.
- A 30-day free trial of Premium, offered on its homepage.


**Pricing:** Premium is $9.99 a month with "No annual commitment, billed monthly", and it adds 4K export and Brand Kits. Adobe publishes no annual price for it.


**Pros:** PDF and transparent PNG on Free, Firefly AI on every plan, no annual commitment for Premium


**Cons:** No native SVG export, 4K export and Brand Kits need Premium, no published annual price


**The no-commitment case:** Premium bills month to month, so a seasonal shop can stay on Free most of the year and pay only in its busy months.


**Final verdict:** Choose Adobe Express for social graphics and PDF flyers, and keep a vector tool for anything that has to scale.


### 10. Placeit


**Overview:** Placeit, from Envato, is built around mockups plus t-shirt and logo templates, exported as PNG, with video exported as MP4. Its license lets you sell "any number of End Products", so there's no copy cap of the kind Kittl puts on Pro and Expert.


What you can't count on is a vector. Placeit's help center lists PNG downloads (MP4 for video), and only its logo page mentions an editable PDF, so its designs suit a fixed-size print-on-demand upload, not a logo that has to grow. That makes it a companion: draw the art elsewhere, then use Placeit for the mockup photos that sell it.


**Key features:**


- Product mockups for the photos on your listings.
- T-shirt and logo templates to start a design from.
- Video templates exported as MP4.


**Pricing:** Placeit costs $14.95 a month or $89.69 a year, about $7.47 a month on the yearly plan. Once you download a file, you're held to a one-month minimum.


**Pros:** Mockups for listings, unlimited end products under its license, video templates too


**Cons:** PNG and MP4 output only per its help center, no SVG, designs start from Placeit's templates, a one-month minimum once you download


**Why sellers try it:** One subscription covers both the shirt design and the mockup photo for the listing, with no print cap.


**Final verdict:** Pick Placeit for listing mockups alongside a vector tool, not as your only design app for merch.


## Which file your printer actually needs


Print-on-demand is why the file format matters to so many sellers.[Grand View Research estimates](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/print-on-demand-market-report) its growth: "The global print on demand market size was valued at USD 10.8 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow from USD 13.1 billion in 2026 to USD 57.5 billion by 2033, at a CAGR of 23.6% from 2026 to 2033."


Every order in that market starts with a file. SVG scales without losing sharpness, so one logo works on a sticker and a banner. PDF carries vectors too, plus print standards such as PDF/X and CMYK, while a 300dpi PNG holds up only at the size you made it.


Check your print-on-demand provider's file guide before you pay for vector export. A flat print at a fixed size may need only a high-resolution PNG, while stickers, embroidery or a logo used at many sizes are where SVG and PDF earn their cost.


Here's the route to those files for each of the nine tools after ours, with Kittl as the baseline, since Awesomic describes no vector export.


Tool Cheapest plan with SVG Its US monthly price PDF export Print-file notes


Kittl (baseline) Pro $19, or $14 billed annually Pro and up CMYK in PDF and JPEG only; SVG always RGB


Affinity Free app $0 Free, including PDF/X CMYK, spot colors, preflight, bleed


Inkscape Free app $0 Free No color-managed export


CorelDRAW Go Its one plan $9.99 per 30 days Yes, same plan Templates from logos to mugs


Recraft Free (personal use only); Basic for commercial use $0; Basic $12, or $10 billed annually Yes Also TIFF and Lottie


Canva Pro $18, or $12 billed annually PDF Print with bleed and crop marks CMYK and transparent PNG on Pro


Adobe Illustrator Its one plan $22.99 on the annual plan Yes, plus AI files Adobe Fonts cleared for merch


Linearity Not itemized $0 Free, $10 Pro; gate unknown Not itemized Curve lists PDF, SVG and AI


Adobe Express None n/a Free Convert to SVG works on uploads only


Placeit None n/a None PNG and MP4; logo page mentions a PDF


So the only free route we could confirm to a CMYK PDF with spot colors and bleed is Affinity, while Inkscape gets you free SVG and PDF without color management. If you generate artwork with AI, ask for flat colors and clean edges at the prompt stage, because in our experience those convert to vectors better than shaded images, and our[prompts for print design](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/the-best-midjourney-prompts-for-print-design-guide) show how we word print prompts.


## License terms to check before you sell merch


Kittl's own terms set the bar. Free is "strictly limited to personal, non-commercial use", and Kittl's pricing page lists a commercial license only from Pro. Pro and Expert allow commercial use, print-on-demand included, up to "500,000 printed copies or 500,000 expected viewers" per design, and Max removes the cap.


A few more Kittl rules catch people out. Publishing a design to the Kittl community transfers its rights to Kittl, and after a Pro or Expert plan ends, Kittl says you can keep using designs "as long as your Kittl account remains open". Kittl also doesn't guarantee that AI output is cleared for commercial use.


The alternatives differ on this. Placeit allows "any number of End Products", Recraft gives commercial rights only from Basic, and Adobe's commercial-safety claim for Express covers its Firefly AI output, not its templates. Canva bars selling a library element as-is on a t-shirt, and Affinity's terms are written for a private individual, pointing companies elsewhere.


Owning a file under a vendor's license isn't the same as holding a copyright in it. The U.S. Copyright Office's January 2025[report on AI copyrightability](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-2-Copyrightability-Report.pdf) concludes that, "given current generally available technology, prompts alone do not provide sufficient human control to make users of an AI system the authors of the output." This isn't legal advice, but prompt-only art may leave you no copyright to enforce.


Whoever makes the art, file each design's license terms with its source files. If you'd rather have a designer draw merch artwork from scratch, our[merch design service](https://www.awesomic.com/merch) has a waitlist open.


## Moving your designs out of Kittl


Vector export needs a paid plan, so move before your Kittl subscription runs out, in this order:


1. Export every design you want to keep as SVG while Pro, Expert or Max is still active.
2. Export a PDF of each print design too, since Kittl's SVGs are always RGB.
3. List the fonts in each design, check each font's license lets you use it outside Kittl, and rebuild any text whose font doesn't come with you.
4. Check Kittl's terms before you reuse anything you published to the Kittl community, since publishing transfers its rights to Kittl.
5. Keep in mind that Kittl doesn't guarantee its AI output is cleared for commercial use, wherever you open the file next.
6. Cancel the paid plan before your renewal date, since Kittl generally doesn't refund a term you've paid for.
7. Keep the Kittl account itself open if you still sell designs made there, because Kittl ties your use of Pro and Expert designs to an open account.


If you're rebuilding a brand kit at the same time, lock its fonts and colors before the first merch file, since every print file inherits them from the kit, whichever of the[branding tools for startups](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/best-branding-tools-for-startups) ends up holding it.


## How to choose by the job you do


Merch sellers should start from the license and the file. Affinity gives you CMYK PDFs for $0 if you work as an individual, since its terms point companies elsewhere, and CorelDRAW Go keeps vector export and product templates for $9.99 per 30 days. Illustrator suits sellers who want Adobe Fonts cleared for merch with no item limit, and Placeit fills in the listing mockups.


Logo work needs a real vector editor, so pick Inkscape if SVG is the deliverable, Affinity if a printer wants CMYK, or Illustrator if you want Adobe's full drawing tools. Recraft helps when you want generated starting points for marks you'll then refine.


Social graphics are the easy case, since a PNG is usually the final file. Adobe Express covers them on Free, and Canva Pro adds SVG and CMYK if the same campaign goes to print. If your team also designs product screens, Canva's freehand and shape tools will feel thin next to a UI tool, the split we draw in[Figma vs Canva](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/figma-vs-canva) .


## Where to start if you're leaving Kittl this month


Export your Kittl library first, then download Affinity and Inkscape, which are both free. Rebuild one real product design in each and send the file to your printer as a test.


If neither fits the way you work, try CorelDRAW Go's 15-day trial or a month of Canva Pro, because they're the closest to Kittl's template habit at a lower price. And if the merch shop needs a website next, our[Durable alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/durable-alternatives) roundup covers the AI site builders.


## FAQ


### Does Kittl's free plan export SVG files?


No. On Free you get PNG and JPG only, capped at 800px and 72dpi, and vector files start on Pro, which costs $19 on monthly billing or $14 a month on a yearly plan.


### Can I sell designs I made on Kittl's free plan?


No. Kittl's license limits Free to "personal, non-commercial use", and its plan grid reserves commercial use for Pro and up. Pro and Expert let you sell up to 500,000 copies of each design, counting printed copies or expected viewers, and Max lifts the cap.


### Which Kittl competitors export CMYK files for print?


Affinity exports CMYK PDFs, including PDF/X, with spot colors, at no cost. Canva offers CMYK on Pro, and Kittl itself offers CMYK only in PDF and JPEG exports. Inkscape doesn't support color management for file export, so check with your printer whether RGB is acceptable.


### Which paid Kittl competitors export SVG most cheaply?


Among paid plans with documented SVG export, CorelDRAW Go's is the cheapest: SVG and PDF for $9.99 per 30 days or $99.99 a year, and Corel is cutting the first period's price for Black Friday this month. Recraft's Basic comes next at $12 monthly, or $10 a month billed annually, and adds commercial rights.


### Is there a Kittl alternative that does the design for me?


Placeit gets you partway with t-shirt and logo templates, though you still edit them yourself. With Awesomic, agents make the asset set, and a designer on the Graphic Pack, a separate $1,799 monthly plan, can take print and packaging work, the same model as a[graphic design subscription](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/graphic-design-subscription) .
